newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Bauxite firm to cut losses in Sierra Leone.
newsitem.headline: Bauxite firm to cut losses in Sierra Leone.

text.p: Bauxite miner SIEROMCO, which provided a fifth of Sierra Leone's vital mineral export earnings until civil war halted its operations last year, has told the government it is pulling out of the West African country.
But Managing Director James Westwood told Reuters in a recent interview that the sale of SIEROMCO's bauxite mine at Mokanji in the south to other investors had not been ruled out.

"Although SIEROMCO will not reopen the mine, we are in touch with two potential investors introduced by the Sierra Leone government...so it would be unfair to say all hope is lost for the future of the mine," he said.

The civilian government that took over in the economically poor but mineral-rich West African country when the army restored democracy after four years of military rule in March is keen to revive the shattered economy.

The Sierra Leone Ore and Metal Company (SIEROMCO), a subsidiary of Swiss aluminium manufacturer Alusuisse, was producing one percent of the world's bauxite from the mine until a rebel attack halted operations in January 1995.
Subsequent looting, widely blamed on government soldiers, caused damage estimated at $30 million.

"At least $20 million will be needed for repairs -- $13 million just for materials -- which in view of the fact there are only 10 years worth of reserves left to mine, is not worth it," Westwood said.

"We are aware of the loss to Sierra Leone and so we have tried everything possible to resume operations but donors such as the World Bank and the European Union will not fund a project which is not seen as economically and technically viable."
Sierra Leone has produced some of the world's finest diamonds, many mined and sold illegally because of the war. Minerals provide most of the country's export earnings.

Sierra Rutile, which once provided almost 60 percent of mineral export earnings, has said it will reopen its rutile mine in 1997 if it can raise around $80 million and make independent security arrangements.
Private South African security company Executive Outcomes, which previously trained the Sierra Leone army to fight the rebels, currently guards its mine.
Rutile or titanium dioxide is of strategic importance in the aerospace industry and is also used in paint pigment.

Westwood, one of 17 foreign nationals held hostage by the rebels for over three months after the attack on the mine, said the need for security spending would make matters even worse. "No bauxite mine in the world has ever had a security force."

Westwood said SIEROMCO was trying to salvage damaged mining equipment, possibly for sale to Sierra Rutile, which is owned by U.S. firm Nord Resources Corp and Australian-based Consolidated Rutile Ltd.

"The difference between SIEROMCO and Rutile is a question of reserves... Rutile is thinking of expanding, which would increase the cost and the risk, but the rewards are potentially higher. SIEROMCO does not have the reserves to play that trick."

SIEROMCO began mining at Mokanji in 1964. In the mid-1980s it exported an average of 1.7 million tons a year. This declined to 1.4 million tons in 1992 and the loss of a major customer in the Ukraine proved a serious blow.
The mine employed 700 people when the rebels attacked.

President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah and rebel leader Foday Sankoh, who took up arms in 1991, agreed to a truce at talks in Ivory Coast but differences over a role for the rebels and their demands for all foreign troops to leave have blocked a permanent deal.
